kkNNProxy: Efficient Training-Free Proxy Alignment
for Black-Box Zero-Shot LLM-Generated Text Detection

Kahim Wong    Kemou Li    Haiwei Wu    and Jiantao Zhou ††thanks: Kahim Wong, Kemou Li, and Jiantao Zhou are with the State Key Laboratory of Internet of Things for Smart City and the Department of Computer and Information Science, Faculty of Science and Technology, University of Macau, Macao 999078, China (e-mail: yc37437@um.edu.mo; kemou.li@connect.umac.mo; jtzhou@umac.mo). (Corresponding author: Jiantao Zhou.) Haiwei Wu is with the School of Information and Software Engineering, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu 611731, China (e-mail: haiweiwu@uestc.edu.cn).
Abstract

LLM-generated text (LGT) detection is essential for reliable forensic analysis and for mitigating LLM misuse. Existing LGT detectors can generally be categorized into two broad classes: learning-based approaches and zero-shot methods. Compared with learning-based detectors, zero-shot methods are particularly promising because they eliminate the need to train task-specific classifiers. However, the reliability of zero-shot methods fundamentally relies on the assumption that an off-the-shelf proxy LLM is well aligned with the often unknown source LLM, a premise that rarely holds in real-world black-box scenarios. To address this discrepancy, existing proxy alignment methods typically rely on supervised fine-tuning of the proxy or repeated interactions with commercial APIs, thereby increasing deployment costs, exposing detectors to silent API changes, and limiting robustness under domain shift. Motivated by these limitations, in this work we propose the kk-nearest neighbor proxy (kkNNProxy), a training-free and query-efficient proxy alignment framework that repurposes the kkNN language model (kkNN-LM) retrieval mechanism as a domain adapter for a fixed proxy LLM. Specifically, a lightweight datastore is constructed once from a target-reflective LGT corpus, either via fixed-budget querying or from existing datasets. During inference, nearest-neighbor evidence induces a token-level predictive distribution that is interpolated with the proxy output, yielding an aligned prediction without proxy fine-tuning or per-token API outputs. To improve robustness under domain shift, we extend kkNNProxy into a mixture of proxies (MoP) that routes each input to a domain-specific datastore for domain-consistent retrieval. Moreover, we theoretically derive a corpus-size-dependent approximation error bound that motivates token-wise adaptive hyperparameters for more reliable detection without costly hyperparameter sweeps. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong detection performance of our method, with an average AUROC of 0.99 across eight recent proprietary LLMs and a 6.45% improvement in AUROC over the prior state-of-the-art (SOTA) alignment method. Beyond binary detection, kkNNProxy also provides strong utility for closed-set LLM source attribution with an average ACC of 0.84. The source code is available at https://github.com/KahimWong/kNNProxy.

Index Terms: 
Large language models, LLM-generated text detection, zero-shot detection, kkNN-LM

I Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress, as exemplified by GPT-5.4 [1], Gemini 3.1 [2], and Claude 4.6 [3], which feature advanced multimodal and reasoning capabilities. Such progress enables a wide range of applications across domains, including customer service [4], healthcare diagnostics [5], and scientific research [6]. However, these advances also introduce critical safety concerns: hallucination, prompt injection vulnerability, and privacy leakage are commonly observed in LLMs, and such issues can result in misinformation and adversarial misuse [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. In particular, LLM-generated text (LGT) poses challenges to trust in digital communication, academic integrity, and information authenticity across society [16]. Consequently, LGT detection, which aims to determine whether a given suspicious text is generated by an LLM or written by a human, emerges as an important challenge for mitigating misuse risks and supporting trustworthy forensics [17, 18].

Existing LGT detection methods identify distinctive characteristics of LGT through either supervised learning [19] or zero-shot approaches [20, 21, 22]. Learning-based detectors rely on labeled human–LLM data to train binary classifiers [23, 24], whereas zero-shot detectors primarily exploit statistical properties of LLMs and generally avoid training task-specific classifiers (cf. Sec. II-A for detailed related works). As illustrated in Fig. 1, zero-shot detection employs a proxy LLM to simulate the source LLM (the LLM responsible for generating the given text) and determines whether the text is LGT based on statistical patterns exhibited by the proxy LLM output. Notably, zero-shot detection is highly sensitive to how accurately the proxy approximates the source LLM; accordingly, strong performance is usually observed only when the proxy output distributions are closely aligned [25, 26] with the source. When the source LLM is known, as in white-box zero-shot detection, such alignment can be readily achieved. In contrast, under the more practical black-box setting where the source LLM is unknown, a single fixed proxy LLM is often insufficient, which makes effective alignment substantially more challenging.

To narrow the alignment gap in black-box zero-shot detection, proxy alignment methods seek to align the proxy LLM with the output distribution of strong proprietary LLMs (i.e., closed-source and commercially owned LLMs). For instance, as illustrated in Fig. 2, DALD [27] aligns the proxy via supervised fine-tuning on text generated by a proprietary LLM, while Glimpse [28] leverages top-kk probabilities returned from commercial APIs to reconstruct an approximate token-level probability distribution that mirrors proprietary model behavior. Despite their effectiveness, existing prevalent methods encounter two practical obstacles that hinder real-world deployment: cost and robustness under domain shift. DALD introduces considerable computational overhead as a result of supervised fine-tuning, while Glimpse is often query-intensive due to repeated interactions with commercial APIs, which expose the method to silent model updates and evolving API behaviors [29]. More critically, both approaches exhibit limited robustness on out-of-domain (OOD) text. DALD typically requires a separately fine-tuned proxy for each domain, whereas Glimpse lacks an explicit mechanism to recalibrate its approximation when the input distribution deviates from the queried data, yielding unreliable alignment on OOD inputs. Taken together, the limitations above motivate the need for a reusable alignment module that can be built with a fixed budget and deployed offline, while remaining adaptable across domains without re-training or continual API access.

In this paper, we propose kkNNProxy, a training-free and query-efficient proxy alignment approach that repurposes kkNN-LM [30] as a retrieval-based domain adapter for a fixed proxy LLM. kkNN-LM augments a parametric LM with a non-parametric datastore of contexts and next tokens. During inference, nearest-neighbor retrieval induces a token-level predictive distribution that can be interpolated into the proxy output. Intuitively, kkNNProxy works because under similar contexts, the proxy and source LLMs differ mainly in token preference and confidence. The datastore stores source-reflective context–next-token evidence, so retrieval provides a lightweight non-parametric correction signal that nudges proxy probabilities toward source-like behavior exactly where zero-shot detectors are most sensitive. Rather than using the retrieval mechanism to improve generation, as is typically done in kkNN-LM, we use it to calibrate detection-time likelihood patterns. This design explains why kkNNProxy can improve robustness under domain shift: when proxy priors become unreliable, retrieved source-reflective neighbors still provide anchored token-level evidence. Specifically, we first construct a datastore from an LGT corpus that reflects the target model, using either fixed-budget querying or existing datasets. Given a suspicious text, we retrieve neighbors at each token position, form a kkNN-induced distribution based on their distances and next-tokens, and interpolate this distribution with the proxy output to obtain an aligned prediction. kkNNProxy yields proxy alignment without fine-tuning or per-input API returns at test time, and it supports scalable domain control by swapping datastores without training multiple proxies. Table I summarizes comparisons between kkNNProxy, fixed-proxy baselines, and prior proxy alignment methods.

To explicitly improve OOD robustness, we further extend kkNNProxy to MoP, an MoE alignment scheme tailored for domain shift. Since a single datastore can become unreliable when test sample drifts away from its indexing datastore, mismatched neighbors may inject misleading next-token evidence and degrade alignment. MoP mitigates this failure mode by maintaining multiple domain-specific datastores as retrieval experts and routing each input to the most compatible expert, enforcing domain-consistent retrieval at test time and yielding more stable proxy–source alignment under domain shift. We further provide a corpus-size-dependent theoretical bound on the approximation error between the source distribution and the aligned distribution. The analysis clarifies when retrieval evidence is trustworthy and directly motivates token-wise adaptive hyperparameters (neighbor size kk and interpolation weight λ\lambda) to improve OOD detection reliability without costly tuning. Beyond LGT detection, the same kkNNProxy mechanism can also be instantiated as multiple source LLM kkNN proxies for closed-set LLM source attribution, highlighting broader forensic utility of our method.

In summary, the contributions of this work are fourfold:

  • •

    Training-free proxy alignment. We propose kkNNProxy, a training-free and query-efficient proxy alignment framework for black-box zero-shot LGT detection that repurposes kkNN-LM as a domain adapter for a fixed proxy LLM, eliminating proxy fine-tuning and avoiding per-input API querying.

  • •

    OOD-robust alignment with domain control. We introduce MoP, an MoE extension that performs domain-consistent retrieval by routing inputs to domain-specific datastores, enhancing robustness under domain shift.

  • •

    Theory-guided adaptive design. We theoretically derive a corpus-size-dependent approximation error bound for retrieval-based alignment and leverage it to develop token-wise adaptive hyperparameters, improving detection while reducing the need for costly hyperparameter sweeps.

  • •

    SOTA detection performance. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves strong detection accuracy, reaching an average AUROC of 0.99 across eight recent proprietary LLMs and improving over the prior SOTA proxy alignment baseline by 6.45% in AUROC.

Organization

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. II reviews related works on learning-based and zero-shot LGT detection. Sec. III describes kkNNProxy and MoP, including datastore construction, retrieval-interpolation alignment, and the MoE-style router for domain control. Sec. IV derives an approximation error bound for the retrieval-induced distribution and motivates token-adaptive hyperparameters. Sec. V reports experimental results and ablations. Finally, Sec. VI concludes the paper.

II Related Work

II-A LGT Detection

Unlike LLM watermarking, which proactively embeds detectable signals into generated text [31, 32], LGT detection identifies LGT without modifying the LLM output, enabling post hoc use on deployed LLMs. Existing passive LGT detection methods are typically grouped into two families: learning-based and zero-shot. Learning-based detectors, such as RoBERTa [19] and XLM-RoBERTa [33], identify LGT by training a binary classifier on large-scale datasets containing both human-written text (HWT) and LGT. However, such methods often exhibit limited OOD generalization and tend to degrade noticeably on unseen topics or texts produced by previously unseen source LLMs [34, 35, 36].

Zero-shot LGT detectors can be further categorized into statistics-, perturbation-, and rewrite-based approaches. (1) Statistics-based methods use a proxy LLM to approximate the source model and compute statistical metrics from the proxy, such as log-likelihood [37], entropy [38], rank [37], log-rank [37], and LRR [39], as surrogates for statistics of the unobserved source model. Binoculars [21] leverages two LLMs and scores text using the ratio of perplexity to cross-perplexity. Lastde [22] analyzes log-likelihood sequences by mining multi-scale diversity entropy. (2) Perturbation-based methods, exemplified by DetectGPT [40], randomly perturb the test sample and distinguishes LGT by comparing log-likelihoods of the original and perturbed through probability curvature. NPR [39] follows a similar spirit by using the ratio of log-ranks before and after perturbation. Fast-DetectGPT [20] further improves the efficiency of DetectGPT by replacing explicit perturbations with conditional probability computations. (3) Rewrite-based methods adopt a different strategy by comparing an input text with regenerated variants. Revise-Detect [41] and RADAR [42] build on the assumption that LLMs revise their own generations less extensively than HWT, and detect LGT by examining discrepancies induced by rewriting. DNA-GPT [43] measures N-gram similarity between truncated original text and regenerated text.

A central limitation of zero-shot detection lies in its strong dependence on the proxy model. Detection performance remains strong only when the proxy distribution closely matches the source LLM, and degrades as the mismatch increases [25, 26]. To mitigate distributional mismatch, several proxy alignment strategies have been explored. DALD [27] fine-tunes the proxy model using text generated from a stronger LLM (e.g., GPT-4) to better align the proxy distribution with the target. In addition, since many commercial black-box APIs provide access to next-token probability, Glimpse [28] reconstructs the entire probability distribution from the top-kk probability returned by proprietary models to support efficient detection. Despite these advances, zero-shot detectors still often exhibit high false-positive rates, and their reliability further declines under post-editing or intentional evasion [44, 45], leaving substantial room for further improvement.

II-B kkNN-LM

kkNN-LM [30] improves the generalizability of pre-trained LLMs by interpolating parametric predictions with non-parametric retrievals from an external datastore, combining implicit model knowledge with explicit memory. This retrieval-augmented design enables flexible, training-free adaptation, making it suitable for dynamic and resource-constrained settings. Building on kkNN-LM, subsequent work focuses on scaling retrieval and broadening applicability. He et al. [46] develop efficient search and caching to reduce inference cost on large datastores. Huang et al. [47] design plug-and-play adapters that enable rapid domain adaptation for black-box LLMs without updating parameters. Other studies investigate when and why kkNN-LM is effective, emphasizing the role of lexical and semantic matching [48] and clarifying its advantages over purely parametric LMs [49]. Beyond standard LLM decoding, kkNN-based retrieval has been used to guide speculative decoding [50]. Recent findings show that kkNN-LM excels on memory-intensive tasks driven by recurring patterns but is less helpful for multi-step reasoning that requires composing new knowledge [51]. Further evidence indicates that kkNN-LM’s gains concentrate on high-frequency tokens, with limited benefits for rare tokens even under long-tail datastores [52].

In contrast to prior studies that apply kkNN-LM to improve generation quality, perplexity, or domain adaptation, our work repurposes kkNN-LM for LGT detection, a discriminative and forensic task rather than a generative one. Here, retrieval supports evidence-driven source analysis instead of improving text generation, thus extending retrieval-augmented modeling to a new application domain. The next section presents our proposed method in detail.

III Methodology

Fig. 3a illustrates the overall workflow of kkNNProxy. Given a suspicious text sequence 𝐱=[x1,…,xT]\mathbf{x}=[x_{1},\ldots,x_{T}], kkNNProxy produces aligned token-level next-token distributions 𝚷^​(𝐱)=[𝝅^(1),…,𝝅^(T)]\hat{\bm{\Pi}}(\mathbf{x})=\bigl[\hat{\bm{\pi}}^{(1)},\ldots,\hat{\bm{\pi}}^{(T)}\bigr], where each 𝝅^(i)∈Δ|𝒱|−1\hat{\bm{\pi}}^{(i)}\in\Delta^{|\mathcal{V}|-1} denotes the aligned prediction at position ii. The sequence is fed into an off-the-shelf zero-shot detector, which evaluates the observed token sequence through the aligned token log-likelihoods ℓi=log⁡π^(i)​(xi)\ell_{i}=\log\hat{\pi}^{(i)}(x_{i}) for i=1,…,Ti=1,\dots,T. A lower-bound clipping rule over {ℓi}i=1T\{\ell_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T} is used to reduce outlier effects and derive the final decision statistic for distinguishing HWT from LGT.

Fig. 3b details how kkNNProxy aligns a fixed proxy LLM MprxM_{\mathrm{prx}} with a stronger proprietary source LLM MsrcM_{\mathrm{src}}. Specifically, a source-reflective corpus is first collected via querying MsrcM_{\mathrm{src}} or reusing existing LGT data, followed by constructing a datastore of context–next-token pairs. At inference, for each position ii, we compute the proxy distribution 𝝅prx(i)\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{prx}}^{(i)}, retrieve kk nearest neighbors from the datastore, and form a retrieval-induced distribution 𝝅knn(i)\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}^{(i)}. 𝝅prx(i)\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{prx}}^{(i)} and 𝝅knn(i)\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}^{(i)} are interpolated to produce the aligned distribution 𝝅^(i)\hat{\bm{\pi}}^{(i)}.

III-A kkNNProxy: kkNN-LM for Proxy LLM Alignment

The goal of kkNNProxy is to approximate the conditional next-token distribution of the unknown source LLM MsrcM_{\mathrm{src}} by a retrieval-augmented proxy, without accessing the source model internals. Formally, at token position ii, we aim to approximate the source distribution 𝝅src(i)=𝝅Msrc(⋅∣𝐱<i)\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}^{(i)}=\bm{\pi}_{M_{\mathrm{src}}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i}). To this end, kkNNProxy builds an offline datastore from a large corpus generated by, or otherwise reflective of, MsrcM_{\mathrm{src}}, as illustrated in Fig. 3b. This corpus can be obtained either by prompting a black-box LLM through APIs or by leveraging existing LGT datasets. Importantly, our method does not require the internal parameters or token-level output probabilities of the source LLM, which makes it more robust to API changes compared to Glimpse.11 1 The default Glimpse relies on access to top-probability outputs from GPT-4 APIs, which are no longer available in the current OpenAI API [29].

III-A1 Offline Datastore Construction

Let 𝒞src\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{src}} denote the collected source-reflective corpus. Using a sliding window of length WW, we construct a datastore ℐ={(𝐡n,yn)}n=1N\mathcal{I}=\{(\mathbf{h}_{n},y_{n})\}_{n=1}^{N}, where 𝐡n∈ℝd\mathbf{h}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a context representation and yn∈𝒱y_{n}\in\mathcal{V} is its corresponding successor token. Concretely, for each local context window 𝐜\mathbf{c} extracted from the corpus, we encode it with the fixed proxy model MprxM_{\mathrm{prx}} and denote the resulting feature vector by 𝐡=ψ⁡(𝐜,Mprx)∈ℝd\mathbf{h}=\psi(\mathbf{c};M_{\mathrm{prx}})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, where ψ⁡(⋅,Mprx)\psi(\cdot;M_{\mathrm{prx}}) is the chosen hidden-state feature extractor of the proxy model. The paired value is the next token immediately following 𝐜\mathbf{c}. After scanning the whole corpus, all keys {𝐡n}n=1N\{\mathbf{h}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} are indexed using FAISS [53] to enable efficient nearest-neighbor retrieval.

III-A2 Retrieval-induced Distribution

Given a suspicious text 𝐱\mathbf{x}, kkNNProxy is applied token by token. At position ii, we first form the query context 𝐜i=[x0,…,xi−1]\mathbf{c}_{i}=[x_{0},\ldots,x_{i-1}], and compute its query representation 𝐪i=ψ⁡(𝐜i,Mprx)∈ℝd\mathbf{q}_{i}=\psi(\mathbf{c}_{i};M_{\mathrm{prx}})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. We then retrieve the index set of its kk nearest neighbors from the datastore, 𝒩k​(𝐪i)⊆{1,…,N}\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q}_{i})\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}. For each retrieved entry j∈𝒩k​(𝐪i)j\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q}_{i}), let 𝐡j\mathbf{h}_{j} be the stored key and yjy_{j} the stored next token. We assign a distance-based weight

αi​j=exp(−dist(𝐪i,𝐡j)/τ)∑l∈𝒩k​(𝐪i)exp(−dist(𝐪i,𝐡l)/τ),j∈𝒩k​(𝐪i),\alpha_{ij}=\frac{\exp\bigl(-\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{q}_{i},\mathbf{h}_{j})/\tau\bigr)}{\sum_{l\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q}_{i})}\exp\bigl(-\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{q}_{i},\mathbf{h}_{l})/\tau\bigr)},\ \ \ \ j\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q}_{i}), (1)

πknn(i)(v)=∑j∈𝒩k​(𝐪i)αi​j 1{yj=v},v∈𝒱,\pi_{\mathrm{knn}}^{(i)}(v)=\sum\nolimits_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q}_{i})}\alpha_{ij}\,\mathbbm{1}\{y_{j}=v\},\quad v\in\mathcal{V}, (2)

𝝅knn(i)=[πknn(i)​(v)]v∈𝒱.\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}^{(i)}=\bigl[\pi_{\mathrm{knn}}^{(i)}(v)\bigr]_{v\in\mathcal{V}}.

III-A3 Aligned Distribution

Meanwhile, the fixed proxy model MprxM_{\mathrm{prx}} produces its own next-token distribution 𝝅prx(i)=𝝅Mprx(⋅∣𝐱<i)\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{prx}}^{(i)}=\bm{\pi}_{M_{\mathrm{prx}}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{<i}). We then interpolate the parametric proxy prediction and the non-parametric retrieval prediction:

𝝅^(i)=λi​𝝅prx(i)+(1−λi)​𝝅knn(i),λi∈[0,1].\hat{\bm{\pi}}^{(i)}=\lambda_{i}\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{prx}}^{(i)}+(1-\lambda_{i})\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}^{(i)},\qquad\lambda_{i}\in[0,1]. (3)

Here λi\lambda_{i} is the interpolation weight. In the basic kkNNProxy formulation, one may simply set λi=λ\lambda_{i}=\lambda as a global constant; later in Sec. IV we further generalize it to a token-adaptive form. Repeating Eq. (3) for i=1,…,Ti=1,\ldots,T yields the aligned distribution sequence 𝚷^​(𝐱)\hat{\bm{\Pi}}(\mathbf{x}).

III-B MoP: Multi-Domain Proxy Alignment

While a single kkNNProxy effectively captures domain-specific patterns for LGT detection, it often underperforms on OOD samples due to limited generalization. To improve robustness under domain shift, we extend kkNNProxy to an MoE variant, MoP, where multiple domain-specific datastores are constructed offline and a lightweight router selects the most compatible expert. As shown in Fig. 4, each expert corresponds to a domain, defined by topic (e.g., academic writing, social media, or news) or source-model family. Since datastore construction in kkNNProxy is training-free and modular, such multi-domain extension is straightforward.

Formally, let {ℐm}m=1M\{\mathcal{I}_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M} be MM domain-specific datastores, where ℐm\mathcal{I}_{m} is built from texts belonging to domain mm and instantiates the mm-th kkNNProxy expert. To select the most compatible expert for a test sample, we build an auxiliary routing datastore. Specifically, from all domain corpora we collect a sentence–domain set {(𝐬n,zn)}n=1Nr\{(\mathbf{s}_{n},z_{n})\}_{n=1}^{N_{\mathrm{r}}}, where 𝐬n\mathbf{s}_{n} is a sentence and zn∈{1,…,M}z_{n}\in\{1,\ldots,M\} is its domain label. Using an off-the-shelf sentence embedding model ϕ\phi, we compute 𝐞n=ϕ⁡(𝐬n)∈ℝdr\mathbf{e}_{n}=\phi(\mathbf{s}_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{r}}}, and form the routing datastore ℐr={(𝐞n,zn)}n=1Nr\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{r}}=\{(\mathbf{e}_{n},z_{n})\}_{n=1}^{N_{\mathrm{r}}}. Given a suspicious text 𝐱\mathbf{x}, we first compute its sentence embedding 𝐞⁡(𝐱)=ϕ⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{e}(\mathbf{x})=\phi(\mathbf{x}), and retrieve its krk_{\mathrm{r}} nearest neighbors in the routing datastore:

𝒩krr​(𝐞⁡(𝐱))⊆{1,…,Nr}.\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{r}}_{k_{\mathrm{r}}}\bigl(\mathbf{e}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{r}}\}. (10)

We then estimate an empirical routing score for each domain mm by majority voting:

ωm(𝐱)=1kr∑n∈𝒩krr​(𝐞⁡(𝐱))𝟙{zn=m},\omega_{m}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{k_{\mathrm{r}}}\sum\nolimits_{n\in\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{r}}_{k_{\mathrm{r}}}(\mathbf{e}(\mathbf{x}))}\mathbbm{1}\{z_{n}=m\}, (11)

where m=1,…,Mm=1,\dots,M. The routed expert index is chosen as

m^​(𝐱)=arg​maxm∈{1,…,M}⁡ωm​(𝐱).\hat{m}(\mathbf{x})=\argmax_{m\in\{1,\ldots,M\}}\omega_{m}(\mathbf{x}). (12)

Finally, we apply the expert associated with ℐm^​(𝐱)\mathcal{I}_{\hat{m}(\mathbf{x})} to produce aligned token distributions and perform downstream detection.

Although one could organize experts by source LLM, we prefer domain/topic partitioning in practice. The reason is that topic structure is often more stable than the rapidly evolving set of commercial LLM versions, and topic-specific retrieval tends to transfer better across unseen or updated source models. As demonstrated in Sec. V, this design yields accurate routing and improved OOD robustness for LGT detection.

III-C Robust Lower-Tail Clipping for Detection Stability

Beyond improving proxy–source alignment, we further stabilize zero-shot detection by replacing the standard arithmetic mean over token scores with a robust lower-bound clipping strategy. Many existing detectors, e.g., likelihood [37], Fast-DetectGPT [20], and Binoculars [21], aggregate token-level evidence by averaging. However, token log-likelihood sequences often contain extreme outliers for both HWT and LGT. As shown in Fig. 5, low-likelihood outliers frequently arise from tokens poorly modeled by the proxy, and can dominate the aggregated score, thereby degrading separability.

To mitigate the effect of outliers, we clip each aligned token log-likelihood from below before averaging. Fig. 5 indicates that the dominant outliers are concentrated in the low-likelihood tail; clipping this tail effectively prevents a few extreme tokens from overwhelming the sequence-level score. Formally, for ℓi=log⁡π^(i)​(xi)\ell_{i}=\log\hat{\pi}^{(i)}(x_{i}), we define the clipped score

ℓ~i=max⁡(ℓi,γ),\tilde{\ell}_{i}=\max(\ell_{i},\gamma), (13)

where γ\gamma is a lower bound. The final sequence statistic is then computed as

ℓ¯γ=1T​∑i=1Tℓ~i.\bar{\ell}_{\gamma}=\frac{1}{T}\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{T}\tilde{\ell}_{i}. (14)

In our experiments, we use a fixed default lower bound γ\gamma. This operation preserves most token-level evidence while suppressing only pathological low-likelihood spikes, and can be directly applied to different zero-shot scoring rules with negligible overhead.

IV Theoretical Analysis of Distribution Discrepancy and Adaptive Parameters in kkNNProxy

We now analyze how accurately the retrieval-induced distribution in kkNNProxy approximates the unknown source distribution. In Sec. IV-A, we first derive a high-probability bound for the discrepancy between the source next-token distribution and the kkNN-induced distribution at a fixed token position. We then use the bound to extract bias and variance surrogates that motivate token-adaptive hyperparameters in Sec. IV-B.

IV-A Error Bound of kkNNProxy

Setup. Fix a query representation 𝐪∈ℝd\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Let ℐ={(𝐡n,yn)}n=1N\mathcal{I}=\{(\mathbf{h}_{n},y_{n})\}_{n=1}^{N} be the datastore, where 𝐡n∈ℝd\mathbf{h}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a context representation and yn∈𝒱y_{n}\in\mathcal{V} is its successor token. For a neighborhood size kk, let 𝒩k​(𝐪)⊆{1,…,N}\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q})\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\} denote the indices of the kk nearest neighbors of 𝐪\mathbf{q} under L2L_{2} distance. Following Eq. (1), the normalized retrieval weights are

αj​(𝐪)=exp(−∥𝐪−𝐡j∥2/τ)∑l∈𝒩k​(𝐪)exp(−∥𝐪−𝐡l∥2/τ),j∈𝒩k​(𝐪),\alpha_{j}(\mathbf{q})=\frac{\exp\left(-\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{h}_{j}\|_{2}/\tau\right)}{\sum\nolimits_{l\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q})}\exp\left(-\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{h}_{l}\|_{2}/\tau\right)},\ \ j\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q}), (15)

where τ>0\tau>0 is the temperature parameter. The corresponding kkNN-induced next-token distribution is

πknn(v∣𝐪)=∑j∈𝒩k​(𝐪)αj(𝐪) 1{yj=v},v∈𝒱.\pi_{\mathrm{knn}}(v\mid\mathbf{q})=\sum\nolimits_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q})}\alpha_{j}(\mathbf{q})\,\mathbbm{1}\{y_{j}=v\},\ \ v\in\mathcal{V}. (16)

To quantify the locality and weight concentration, define

keff​(𝐪)≔1∑j∈𝒩k​(𝐪)αj​(𝐪)2∈[1,k],k_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{q})\coloneq\frac{1}{\sum\nolimits_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q})}\alpha_{j}(\mathbf{q})^{2}}\in[1,k], (17)

and the effective neighborhood radius

reff​(𝐪)≔∑j∈𝒩k​(𝐪)αj​(𝐪)​‖𝐪−𝐡j‖2.r_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{q})\coloneq\sum\nolimits_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q})}\alpha_{j}(\mathbf{q})\,\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{h}_{j}\|_{2}. (18)

We also define the conditional mean estimator

π¯knn​(v∣𝐪)≔\displaystyle\bar{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}(v\mid\mathbf{q})\coloneq{} 𝔼⁡[πknn​(v∣𝐪)|{𝐡j}j∈𝒩k​(𝐪)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\pi_{\mathrm{knn}}(v\mid\mathbf{q})\,\middle|\,\{\mathbf{h}_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q})}\right] (19)
=\displaystyle={} ∑j∈𝒩k​(𝐪)αj​(𝐪)​πsrc​(v∣𝐡j),\displaystyle\sum\nolimits_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q})}\alpha_{j}(\mathbf{q})\,\pi_{\mathrm{src}}(v\mid\mathbf{h}_{j}),

where 𝝅src(⋅∣𝐡)\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{h}) denotes the source next-token distribution at representation 𝐡\mathbf{h}. For brevity, below we write V≔|𝒱|V\coloneq|\mathcal{V}| and

𝒩≔𝒩k​(𝐪),αj≔αj​(𝐪),keff≔keff​(𝐪),reff≔reff​(𝐪).\mathcal{N}\coloneq\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{q}),\ \alpha_{j}\coloneq\alpha_{j}(\mathbf{q}),\ k_{\mathrm{eff}}\coloneq k_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{q}),\ r_{\mathrm{eff}}\coloneq r_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{q}).
Assumption 1 (Local Smoothness and Conditional Sampling).

The source next-token distribution satisfies:

  1. 1.

    L1L_{1}-Lipschitz Continuity:

    ∥𝝅src(⋅∣𝐡′)−𝝅src(⋅∣𝐡)∥1≤L∥𝐡′−𝐡∥2,∀𝐡,𝐡′∈ℝd.\bigl\|\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{h}^{\prime})-\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{h})\bigr\|_{1}\leq L\,\|\mathbf{h}^{\prime}-\mathbf{h}\|_{2},\quad\forall\,\mathbf{h},\mathbf{h}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
  2. 2.

    Conditional Independence of Retrieved Tokens: conditioned on the retrieved keys {𝐡j}j∈𝒩\{\mathbf{h}_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{N}}, the tokens {yj}j∈𝒩\{y_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{N}} are independent and satisfy

    yj∼𝝅src(⋅∣𝐡j),j∈𝒩.y_{j}\sim\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{h}_{j}),\quad j\in\mathcal{N}.

Assum. 1 is standard and mild in our setting. Assum. 1.1 states that nearby context representations should induce similar source distributions, which is exactly the smoothness needed for local retrieval to be meaningful. Assum. 1.2 matches the datastore construction process: once the retrieved contexts are fixed, their next tokens are treated as draws from the corresponding source conditional distributions.

Theorem 1 (L1L_{1} Bound for Weighted kkNN Retrieval).

Under Assum. 1, for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

∥𝝅src(⋅∣𝐪)−𝝅knn(⋅∣𝐪)∥1≤Lreff+Vlog⁡(2​V/δ)2​keff.\bigl\|\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})-\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})\bigr\|_{1}\leq Lr_{\mathrm{eff}}+V\sqrt{\frac{\log(2V/\delta)}{2\,k_{\mathrm{eff}}}}. (20)
Proof.

Let 𝝅¯knn(⋅∣𝐪)\bar{\bm{\pi}}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q}) denote the vector form of π¯knn​(v∣𝐪)\bar{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}(v\mid\mathbf{q}). By the triangle inequality,

∥𝝅src(⋅∣𝐪)−𝝅knn(⋅∣𝐪)∥1≤∥𝝅src(⋅∣𝐪)−𝝅¯knn(⋅∣𝐪)∥1⏟bias\displaystyle\bigl\|\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})-\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})\bigr\|_{1}\leq\underbrace{\bigl\|\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})-\bar{\bm{\pi}}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})\bigr\|_{1}}_{\text{bias}} (21)
+∥𝝅¯knn(⋅∣𝐪)−𝝅knn(⋅∣𝐪)∥1⏟variance.\displaystyle+\underbrace{\bigl\|\bar{\bm{\pi}}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})-\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})\bigr\|_{1}}_{\text{variance}}.

For the bias term, Eq. (19) and Assum. 1.1 give

∥𝝅src(⋅∣𝐪)−𝝅¯knn(⋅∣𝐪)∥1\displaystyle\bigl\|\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})-\bar{\bm{\pi}}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})\bigr\|_{1} (22)
=‖∑j∈𝒩αj(𝝅src(⋅∣𝐪)−𝝅src(⋅∣𝐡j))‖1\displaystyle=\left\|\sum\nolimits_{j\in\mathcal{N}}\alpha_{j}\bigl(\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})-\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{h}_{j})\bigr)\right\|_{1}
≤∑j∈𝒩αj∥𝝅src(⋅∣𝐪)−𝝅src(⋅∣𝐡j)∥1\displaystyle\leq\sum\nolimits_{j\in\mathcal{N}}\alpha_{j}\bigl\|\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})-\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{src}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{h}_{j})\bigr\|_{1}
≤L​∑j∈𝒩αj​‖𝐪−𝐡j‖2=L​reff.\displaystyle\leq L\sum\nolimits_{j\in\mathcal{N}}\alpha_{j}\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{h}_{j}\|_{2}=L\,r_{\mathrm{eff}}.

For the variance term, fix v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V} and define

ξj(v)≔𝟙{yj=v}−πsrc(v∣𝐡j),j∈𝒩.\xi_{j}^{(v)}\coloneq\mathbbm{1}\{y_{j}=v\}-\pi_{\mathrm{src}}(v\mid\mathbf{h}_{j}),\quad j\in\mathcal{N}.

Conditioned on {𝐡j}j∈𝒩\{\mathbf{h}_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{N}}, variables {ξj(v)}j∈𝒩\{\xi_{j}^{(v)}\}_{j\in\mathcal{N}} are independent, mean-zero, and each lies in an interval of length 11. Since

πknn​(v∣𝐪)−π¯knn​(v∣𝐪)=∑j∈𝒩αj​ξj(v),\pi_{\mathrm{knn}}(v\mid\mathbf{q})-\bar{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}(v\mid\mathbf{q})=\sum\nolimits_{j\in\mathcal{N}}\alpha_{j}\,\xi_{j}^{(v)},

Hoeffding’s inequality for weighted sums gives

Pr⁡(|πknn​(v∣𝐪)−π¯knn​(v∣𝐪)|≥t|{𝐡j}j∈𝒩)\displaystyle\Pr\big(|\pi_{\mathrm{knn}}(v\mid\mathbf{q})-\bar{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}(v\mid\mathbf{q})|\geq t\,\big|\,\{\mathbf{h}_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{N}}\big) (23)
≤2​exp⁡(−2​t2∑j∈𝒩αj2)=2​exp⁡(−2​keff​t2).\displaystyle\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{2t^{2}}{\sum\nolimits_{j\in\mathcal{N}}\alpha_{j}^{2}}\right)=2\exp\bigl(-2k_{\mathrm{eff}}t^{2}\bigr).

If ∥𝝅knn(⋅∣𝐪)−𝝅¯knn(⋅∣𝐪)∥1≥ε\bigl\|\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})-\bar{\bm{\pi}}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})\bigr\|_{1}\geq\varepsilon, then at least one coordinate must satisfy

|πknn​(v∣𝐪)−π¯knn​(v∣𝐪)|≥εV.\left|\pi_{\mathrm{knn}}(v\mid\mathbf{q})-\bar{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}(v\mid\mathbf{q})\right|\geq\frac{\varepsilon}{V}.

Applying a union bound over v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V} yields

Pr(∥𝝅knn(⋅∣𝐪)−𝝅¯knn(⋅∣𝐪)∥1≥ε|{𝐡j}j∈𝒩)\displaystyle\Pr\left(\bigl\|\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})-\bar{\bm{\pi}}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})\bigr\|_{1}\geq\varepsilon\,\middle|\,\{\mathbf{h}_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{N}}\right) (24)
≤\displaystyle\leq{} ∑v∈𝒱Pr⁡(|πknn​(v∣𝐪)−π¯knn​(v∣𝐪)|≥εV|{𝐡j}j∈𝒩)\displaystyle\sum\nolimits_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\Pr\left(\left|\pi_{\mathrm{knn}}(v\mid\mathbf{q})-\bar{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}(v\mid\mathbf{q})\right|\geq\frac{\varepsilon}{V}\,\middle|\,\{\mathbf{h}_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{N}}\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq{} 2​V​exp⁡(−2​keff​ε2V2).\displaystyle 2V\exp\left(-\frac{2k_{\mathrm{eff}}\varepsilon^{2}}{V^{2}}\right).

Setting the RHS to δ\delta gives, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

∥𝝅knn(⋅∣𝐪)−𝝅¯knn(⋅∣𝐪)∥1≤Vlog⁡(2​V/δ)2​keff.\bigl\|\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})-\bar{\bm{\pi}}_{\mathrm{knn}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{q})\bigr\|_{1}\leq V\sqrt{\frac{\log(2V/\delta)}{2\,k_{\mathrm{eff}}}}. (25)

Combining Eqs. (21), (22), and (25) proves Eq. (20). ∎

Remark.

Thm. 1 separates the retrieval error into a local bias term L​reffLr_{\mathrm{eff}} and a variance term of order keff−1/2k_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1/2}. It therefore suggests that retrieval is most accurate when the selected neighbors are both close to the query and not overly concentrated on a few samples. These two quantities will be the key proxies for designing adaptive hyperparameters in Sec. IV-B.

IV-B Token-adaptive kkNNProxy Hyperparameters

Thm. 1 shows that the retrieval error at query 𝐪\mathbf{q} is governed by two local quantities: the effective radius reff​(𝐪)r_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{q}) and the effective neighborhood size keff​(𝐪)k_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{q}). This suggests that a single global choice of hyperparameters may be suboptimal across different token positions. Intuitively, in dense regions, using more neighbors and smoother weights can reduce variance with only a limited increase in bias. In sparse regions, by contrast, large neighborhoods or overly smooth weights may place nontrivial mass on distant and less relevant keys, thereby increasing bias. Motivated by this trade-off, we make the neighborhood size kk, the retrieval temperature τ\tau, and the interpolation weight λ\lambda adaptive to each query representation.

Adaptive kk and τ\tau. Guided by Eq. (20), we define the following surrogate for the local retrieval error:

𝒰⁡(k,τ,𝐪)≔c​reff​(k,τ,𝐪)+1keff​(k,τ,𝐪),\mathcal{U}(k,\tau;\mathbf{q})\coloneq c\,r_{\mathrm{eff}}(k,\tau;\mathbf{q})+\frac{1}{\sqrt{k_{\mathrm{eff}}(k,\tau;\mathbf{q})}}, (26)

where c>0c>0 is a global calibration coefficient. This objective mirrors the bias–variance structure in Thm. 1: the first term penalizes nonlocal retrieval, whereas the second penalizes overly concentrated weights. Since the constants in Eq. (20), such as LL, VV, and δ\delta, are either unknown or fixed across queries, we absorb their relative scaling into cc.

We then select the token-wise retrieval hyperparameters by

(k∗​(𝐪),τ∗​(𝐪))∈arg​mink∈𝒦,τ∈𝒯⁡𝒰​(k,τ,𝐪),(k^{*}(\mathbf{q}),\tau^{*}(\mathbf{q}))\in\argmin_{k\in\mathcal{K},\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{U}(k,\tau;\mathbf{q}), (27)

where 𝒦\mathcal{K} and 𝒯\mathcal{T} are predefined candidate sets. In practice, for each query we retrieve the top-kmaxk_{\max} neighbors only once, and then evaluate Eq. (27) over all candidate pairs (k,τ)(k,\tau) using truncated prefixes of this ranked list. Consequently, stable local regions tend to favor larger kk and smoother weighting, while sparse or unreliable regions prefer smaller neighborhoods and sharper weighting.

Adaptive λ\lambda. After determining k∗​(𝐪)k^{*}(\mathbf{q}) and τ∗​(𝐪)\tau^{*}(\mathbf{q}), we use the resulting local retrieval quality to adapt the interpolation weight in Eq. (3). Recall that λ\lambda weights the proxy distribution 𝝅prx(i)\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{prx}}^{(i)}, while 1−λ1-\lambda weights the retrieval distribution 𝝅knn(i)\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}^{(i)}. Therefore, a more reliable retrieval estimate should lead to a smaller λ\lambda. Using the optimized retrieval parameters, define

𝒰∗​(𝐪)≔𝒰⁡(k∗​(𝐪),τ∗​(𝐪),𝐪).\mathcal{U}^{*}(\mathbf{q})\coloneq\mathcal{U}\bigl(k^{*}(\mathbf{q}),\tau^{*}(\mathbf{q});\mathbf{q}\bigr). (28)

We then convert this quantity into an adaptive interpolation weight through a sigmoid mapping:

λ∗​(𝐪)=σ⁡(𝒰∗​(𝐪)−median⁡{𝒰∗​(𝐪′):𝐪′∈𝒬⁡(𝐱)}),\lambda^{*}(\mathbf{q})=\sigma\bigl(\mathcal{U}^{*}(\mathbf{q})-\operatorname{median}\{\mathcal{U}^{*}(\mathbf{q}^{\prime}):\mathbf{q}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Q}(\mathbf{x})\}\bigr), (29)

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function, median\operatorname{median} denotes the median operator, and 𝒬⁡(𝐱)={𝐪1,…,𝐪T}\mathcal{Q}(\mathbf{x})=\{\mathbf{q}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{q}_{T}\} is the set of query representations extracted from the input text 𝐱\mathbf{x}. As a result, tokens with below-median surrogate error receive smaller λ∗\lambda^{*} and rely more on 𝝅knn\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{knn}}, whereas tokens with above-median surrogate error receive larger λ∗\lambda^{*} and fall back more heavily on 𝝅prx\bm{\pi}_{\mathrm{prx}}. This yields a simple and effective token-adaptive instantiation of kkNNProxy.

V Experiments

V-A Settings

We evaluate kkNNProxy on the Mix8 [28, 54] and DetectRL [34] benchmarks, with Table II summarizing the benchmark details. All experiments are conducted in the black-box setting, where the proxy LLM used by the detector is different from the source LLM that generated the test samples. We report the AUROC and F1 score (higher the better), which are standard metrics in LLM-generated text detection [34, 28].

V-A1 Mix8 Benchmarking

We construct the Mix8 benchmark by combining test sets from Glimpse [28] and DNA-DetectLLM [54], resulting in a unified suite that covers eight latest commercial LLMs. The Glimpse test set covers three domains, including XSum [55], WritingPrompts [56], and PubMedQA [57]. For each domain, we randomly sample 150 HWTs and generate LGTs by prompting each source model with the 30-token prefix of the same texts. The Glimpse test set includes five source LLMs, including GPT-3.5, GPT-4 [58], Claude-3 Sonnet/Opus [59], and Gemini-1.5 Pro [60]. DNA-DetectLLM complements this setup with 150 sampled HWTs spanning XSum [55], WritingPrompts [56], and arXiv [61], paired with three more recent proprietary models, GPT-4 Turbo [62], Gemini-2.0 Flash [63], and Claude-3.7 Sonnet [64].

V-A2 DetectRL Benchmarking

DetectRL [34] covers 4 domains, including arXiv [61], XSum [55], WritingPrompts [56] and Yelp Reviews [65]. LGT is generated by GPT-3.5 Turbo [66], PaLM-2-Bison [67], Claude Instant 1.2 [68], and Llama-2-70B [69]. Crucially, DetectRL includes a large number of attack-augmented test samples beyond direct prompting, including prompt-based, paraphrase, and perturbation attacks.

V-A3 Competitors

We compare kkNNProxy against 11 zero-shot detectors, including Likelihood [37], Entropy [38], Rank [37], LogRank [37], LRR [39], NPR [39], Revise-Detect [41], DNA-GPT [43], DetectGPT [40], Fast-DetectGPT [20], and Binoculars [21]. Each detector is evaluated with its default proxy LLM, including GPT-Neo-2.7B [70], GPT-J-6B [71], T5-11B [72], Llama-2-7B [69], Falcon-7B [73], and Falcon-7B-Instruct [74] (cf. Table III), as well as 2 proxy alignment methods, DALD [27] (with their open-source aligned Llama-2-7B [75]) and Glimpse [28] with DaVinci-002 API [76].

V-A4 Implementation Details

For Mix8, we build the datastore with the GPT-4 responses in WildChat [77], matching the same training set used by DALD [27] for a fair comparison. For DetectRL, we use the training split to construct the datastore. For MoP, we use NV-Embed-v2 [78] to obtain sentence embeddings for routing. All experiments are run on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU.

V-B Results on Mix8

Table III reports AUROC on the Mix8 benchmark, where results for each source LLM are averaged over three topic domains. Overall, our strongest instantiation (Binoculars detector ♢\diamondsuit with proxy LLMs Falcon-7B + Falcon-7B-Instruct⋆, ⋆{\star} denotes the aligned LLM) achieves the best performance across all source LLMs, reaching an average AUROC of 0.990. Compared with the default Binoculars setting (0.974), the relative improvement is 1.64% under the same proxy LLM pair. In contrast, combining Binoculars with DALD yields 0.866 average AUROC, indicating a relative decrease of 11.09% versus the original Binoculars detector.

Among zero-shot methods, classic methods such as Rank and Entropy exhibit limited separability on modern closed models, whereas the latest detectors, such as Fast-DetectGPT and Binoculars are substantially stronger. Therefore, we further instantiate Fast-DetectGPT ♠\spadesuit and Binoculars ♢\diamondsuit with aligned proxy LLMs to compare different proxy-alignment strategies. Notably, Glimpse relies on top-kk probabilities returned by the API to approximate the full next-token distributions which can be fragile in practice. For example, the GPT-4 API no longer returns top-kk probabilities [29], so we mark the corresponding entries as “-”. For Fast-DetectGPT, all alignment strategies improve over its original zero-shot baseline of 0.893. DALD reaches 0.923 with a gain of 3.36%. Glimpse with DaVinci-002 reaches 0.930 with a gain of 4.14%. kkNNProxy achieves the best AUROC of 0.954 with a gain of 6.83%. The results demonstrate that kkNNProxy provides a more reliable proxy alignment mechanism that leverages corpus retrieval to strengthen black-box LGT detection across a broad set of proprietary LLMs.

V-C Results on DetectRL

V-C1 In-domain Evaluation

Table IV reports the in-domain results on DetectRL under the Multi-Topic and Multi-LLM settings, in which kkNNProxy uses the in-domain training set to build the datastore. We instantiate kkNNProxy on top of multiple zero-shot detectors and observe consistent gains in both settings. Our strongest instantiation, Binoculars ♢\diamondsuit + kkNNProxy, reaches near-ceiling AUROC at 0.999 for Multi-Topic and 0.998 for Multi-LLM. The improvement is not limited to a single baseline. Likelihood improves by about 56%, Fast-DetectGPT improves by roughly 66–71%, and even Binoculars still gains around 15–20%. In addition, the original Binoculars setting shows notable cross-LLM variance in Multi-LLM, dropping to 0.552 on Claude, while kkNNProxy remains consistently strong across different source LLMs. These results suggest that aligning the proxy distribution with a retrieval-augmented distribution yields a reliable detection signal that remains stable across different topics and source-LLMs, especially with attack-augmented test samples.

V-C2 Out-of-domain Evaluation

Beyond the in-domain evaluation, we further stress-test the detectors under the out-of-domain setting on DetectRL, with F1 score results reported in Table V. For kkNNProxy, we use a single unified threshold across all LLMs and topics. We find that kkNNProxy remains effective under distribution shift. Our strongest variant, ♢\diamondsuit + kkNNProxy, reaches a mean F1 score of about 0.91 in both Multi-LLM and Multi-Topic. Relative to the original Binoculars baseline, this translates to a clear gain of roughly 17–23%. The effect is even more pronounced for Fast-DetectGPT, where alignment boosts F1 score from around 0.3–0.4 to about 0.79, especially in Multi-LLM. Overall, these results show that kkNNProxy yields a substantially more stable detection signal under combined topic shifts, source-LLM shifts, and attack perturbations.

V-C3 MoP Results

Additionally, we evaluate the effectiveness of our MoP design for cross-topic generalization. For each source topic, we build three topic-specific kkNNProxy ​​s using the training sets of the remaining topics as the retrieval corpora, and use the topic router (Sec. III-B) to dispatch each test sample to the most suitable topic-specific kkNNProxy. As reported in the last two rows in Table V, MoP achieves the average F1 score of 0.798 for ♠\spadesuit + MoP and 0.911 for ♢\diamondsuit + MoP, showing that routing across domain-specific proxies can further improve OOD robustness. To assess the accuracy of the MoE router, we show the confusion matrices in Fig. 6 under two settings: including and excluding the source topic. Using a sentence-embedding model with a kkNN router, we achieve over 0.97 routing accuracy across the four topics. When the source topic is excluded, the router assigns each test sample to its most similar topic, and the results align with the topical readability and lexical distribution of DetectRL.

V-D Ablation Studies

V-D1 kkNNProxy Hyperparameters

We analyze the sensitivity of kkNNProxy to 5 key hyperparameters in Fig. 7. (1) Temperature: The temperature parameter τ\tau controls how sharply retrieval weights concentrate on nearest neighbors. With fixed values, performance improves from 0.877 at τ=0.1\tau=0.1 to a peak of 0.906 at τ=5\tau=5, then drops to 0.895 at larger values τ=50\tau=50. The adaptive-temperature variant further improves performance to 0.911. (2) Neighbor Size kk: We vary kk from 16 to 1024 and evaluate the adaptive-kk strategy. Fixed-kk performance is relatively stable in the 0.899–0.906 range, with the best fixed point at k=256k=256. The adaptive-kk variant achieves 0.911 and outperforms all fixed settings. (3) Interpolation Weight λ\lambda: The interpolation weight controls how much the retrieval distribution contributes to the final distribution. Recall that a smaller λ\lambda means a larger contribution from the retrieval distribution. As λ\lambda decreases from 1 to 0.1, AUROC improves consistently from 0.810 to 0.905, and adaptive λ\lambda reaches the best value of 0.911. (4) Clip Value γ\gamma: We study clipping to suppress extreme low-confidence token effects. Starting from 0.911 without clipping, AUROC increases as clipping becomes moderately stronger and reaches the best value 0.943 at γ=−7.5\gamma=-7.5. Overly aggressive clipping then hurts performance, dropping to 0.916 at γ=−5.0\gamma=-5.0. (5) Corpus Size NN: We study how the size of the domain corpus used to build the datastore affects performance. Larger corpora consistently improve AUROC, from 0.879 at 1 × 104{}^{\text{4}} to 0.943 with the full corpus 6 × 106{}^{\text{6}}, confirming that richer domain coverage provides more reliable neighbor evidence and strengthens proxy alignment.

V-D2 Proxy-related Ablation

Table VI studies three proxy-related factors in kkNNProxy. Following Glimpse, we apply prompt concatenation before test samples, and the prompt templates are listed in Table VII. We report the detection AUROC for five black-box target LLMs, along with the average AUROC. (1) Corpus Source LLM: The source LLM used to build the retrieval corpus strongly affects performance. As the corpus source becomes stronger, the average AUROC rises from 0.897 (Claude) to 0.953 (GPT-4), showing that higher-quality source-reflective corpora provide more effective alignment signals. (2) Prompt Template: Prompt formatting also contributes. Prompt 2 (in Table VII) achieves the best average AUROC of 0.961, while the other prompts remain close in the 0.953–0.959 range, indicating that concatenating role-aware context provides a consistent but moderate gain. (3) Base Proxy LLM: The base proxy choice has a clear impact. Falcon-7B-Instruct performs best with 0.953 average AUROC, followed by GPT-Neo-2.7B at 0.941. Other candidates are weaker, including Llama-2-7B at 0.924, Llama-3.1-8B at 0.913, and Falcon-7B at 0.836.

V-E LLM Source Attribution

We further show that kkNNProxy is not limited to LGT detection, but can also be used for closed-set LLM source attribution. Given a set of source LLMs, we construct a distinct kkNNProxy for each source LLM using the source-LLM-generated corpus. At inference time, we compute the log-likelihood of the test samples under every kkNNProxy and predict the source as the model with the highest likelihood. To evaluate attribution accuracy, we conduct experiments on the DetectRL multi-LLM split, which contains 4 LLMs, including GPT-3.5 Turbo, PaLM-2-Bison, Claude-Instant, and Llama-2-70B. For each LLM, we use the training split to build the datastore, and evaluate on the test split with the confusion matrix shown in Fig. 8. kkNNProxy delivers strong closed-set source attribution, achieving an average accuracy of 0.84 across the four LLMs. In particular, it attributes Llama-2 and PaLM-2 reliably with accuracies of 0.94 and 0.88, respectively, while remaining competitive on GPT-3.5 and Claude. Specifically, most mistakes come from confusing Claude with Llama-2 or PaLM-2, which is consistent with DetectRL observations that Claude/PaLM/Llama generations have similar readability statistics and can be harder to separate.

V-F Visualization

We illustrate how kkNNProxy alignment changes the token-level log-likelihood landscape in Fig. 9. Without kkNNProxy, the HWT receive even higher scores than the LGT, suggesting limited separability when the proxy distribution is not well aligned to the source generator. After applying kkNNProxy, the per-token log-likelihood patterns and the overall score become more differentiated. Retrieval injects corpus-supported next-token evidence into the proxy distribution, which modifies token confidences in a context-dependent manner and yields a more stable scoring signal for black-box LGT detection.

VI Conclusion

We present kkNNProxy, a training-free and query-efficient proxy alignment approach for black-box LGT detection that leverages kkNN-LM retrieval as an adapter for a fixed proxy LLM. By constructing a datastore and using nearest-neighbor retrieval to induce a source-aware distribution that is blended with the proxy output, kkNNProxy aligns proxy–source LLMs without fine-tuning or intensive API queries. To further handle domain shift, we introduce MoP that routes each input to a domain-specific expert, and develop a theoretical analysis of the kkNNProxy approximation error, motivating token-wise adaptive kkNNProxy hyperparameters. Finally, extensive experiments on challenging modern benchmarks for LGT detection demonstrate that kkNNProxy can provide a stable detection signal under both topic and source LLM shifts.
